title: The Fox X-Men movies should be the blueprint for how to do "dark" superhero movies

commenti.body: I was thinking about these films just last night. Almost started watching them again. I agree, these films were done very well, yet they hardly ever get talked about as good examples of the genre. It's almost like they were taken for granted because we didn't have many superhero films to compare them to 20-25 years ago.
The success of X-Men is what really kick-started all the SuperHero movies and gave Marvel the confidence for MCU.

I loved loved loved X 1 and 2 as a kid. Born in ‘92. Raimi Spiderman, an actual Hulk movie, and Batman Begins; those were the best of times. Hellboy too. It really feels these days like the 2nd golden age of superhero movies is over. Hopefully in the future we have more directors who can innovate and tell unique super stories. But these days things have definitely stagnated.

It could be mostly due to the so-so entries in the franchise. The first two are legitimately good movies, cheesy lines aside. X3 was an odd conclusion that left fans divided. Wolverine Origins was terrible. The Wolverine is forgettable. First Class and Days of Future Past are well received, but Apocalypse and Dark Phoenix are not particularly well received. Logan was great and the Deadpool movies are also great. 

It’s all just very dicey but I think the good ones get plenty of love and appreciation for what they did for the genre. Same goes for Raimi’s first two Spider-Man films.

I definitely see the similarities between Raimi's first two Spiderman films and the first two X-Men films. They occupy similar ground. 

And I wonder if that ground is... that despite being excellent films that quietly kickstarted a genre, both of their influences got passed over in the long term evolution of superhero movies?

Seems like Nolan's Dark Knight became the blueprint for the moody lone superhero film, while The Avengers' fast-talking, RDJ-smirky humor type stuff became the blueprint for group superhero movies.

If you were around back then, you'll know that X-Men and Spiderman weren't even called superhero movies. They were comic-book movies. 

The only one that bucked the trend for me was Watchmen, which I would say is a comic-book movie rather than a superhero movie.

It’s interesting you talk about the fox x-men movies without bringing up Logan. I think that’s the single best superhero movie out there in how it meaningfully and emotionally grounded it is. Just a tarting with showing how different it is in image, old man Logan is a very deliberate and surprising contrast to Jackman’s super-muscular hypermasculine Wolverine character in previous films, and the gruffness is a lot more compelling seeing him as this withered old man who has these brutal fights that leave him totally out of breath as shown in the opening, and the position he’s in working the lowly jobs he does now. 

I think it’s an incredibly mature way to build on a genre and end a franchise, especially by bringing back Patrick Stewart as Professor X but having him be drastically changed from the assuring paternal professorial leader figure he was in earlier films. More so, I think the film does well ok not needing to stand on what comes before—context is helpful, but it’s not as though you need to see every single wolverine and X-men film before it so much as just get a general impression of the characters and tone to see how much it’s changed. I think especially commendable is the emotional dynamic between Jackman and Dadne Keen’s acting. She’s a very deserving co-star, and the relationship between the two is compelling in the generational lineage.

As another, more recently relevant point of praise, I think that it handled its mature themes and rating quite well. The only other R-rated superhero films that come to mind are Deadpool, which plays its explicit and bloody content off for comedy, and Multiverse of madness, which was, charitably, messy. The violence of Logan isn’t glamorized, cool or positioned as spectacle like so many other but is gritty, clumsy, and if I’m not reading too deeply into it, very calculatedly uncomfortable in watching old Hugh Jackman, well out of his age and presentation to be this sort of character, inflicting this kind of brutal violence, getting winded, beat up, and even shooting up so he can sprint a bit and fight some more in the last part of the movie.

On top of that, I think it really does an excellent job of an ending a franchise/character well. There is a surprising amount of dignity in the movie removed from the usual superhero tropes and plot beats, which the film itself already departs from, and there is this interesting interaction with Jackman’s character’s lineage and where he is now, as the children characters are curious at hearing the legends of wolverine and seeing this withered old man who doesn’t give a damn about that image, though clearly is aware of how different he appears now. The X-grave is a very nice touch in the end, and I think particularly good as both fan-payment and memorial.

I 100% agree with everything you wrote, I just left Logan off of the post because I haven't gotten to rewatching it yet, same for everything that came out after 2011 (The Wolverine, Apocalypse, and Dark Phoenix for Examples). I didn't want to include anything that I hadn't seen within the last month while trying to make a point
I normally think of Spider man as kickstarting it off, but I always forget X1 came out a solid 2 years beforehand

The Wolverine (Director's Cut) is really underrated man. It has some amazing Wolverine action and some real appreciation for Japan unlike most Hollywood films that are just set in "a different country". It's honestly one of my favorite X-Men films out there. Just my two cents.

I recently rewatched *X-MEN: APOCALYPSE* (a film everyone on the Internet complains about but I personally love) and I still can't believe the amount of stuff they were able to get away with despite being PG-13. It's not as bloody as *DEADPOOL* or *LOGAN*, but it gets pretty intense in so many scenes and the parts that do show blood will make you cringe a little bit in an *"oh Lord! That must've hurt"* way. It was specially refreshing to see at a time when the rating got more restricted by studios in terms of what was brutal and what wasn't. Blood and bruises have become very standard in battle scenes, but it has come to a point in which it doesn't have weight because the characters always act like nothing happens.

One of my favorite parts about Mark Steven Johnson's *DAREDEVIL* and Louis Leterrier's *THE INCREDIBLE HULK* is that when the characters get hurt, you do feel their pain. Their injuries have an impact on the plot. There's a great scene in *DAREDEVIL* in which Matt gets back to his apartment and you really feel how painful it must be for him to this every night. And in *THE INCREDIBLE HULK* (particularly in Edward Norton's script), the theme of *"physical wounds leaving marks"* is present throughout the movie. There're several deleted scenes that show how Bruce is affected by the image of an unconscious Betty bleeding in her forehead.

While I do understand that a lot of X-Men fans didn't like certain changes, it's a shame that a lot of people have turned their back on these movies simply because now Marvel owns the X-Men. The first two were huge gambles and they managed to make it into a lot of people's favorite superhero films lists back then. People focus way too much on the ones they didn't like and generalize the franchise as if all the films were some kind of abomination. It's specially baffling when films like *X-MEN: DAYS OF FUTURE PAST* and *LOGAN* exist. Personally, I've loved the majority of films in this universe.
